newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk police hold Kurd rebels for suicide bomb.
newsitem.headline: Turk police hold Kurd rebels for suicide bomb.

text.p: Turkish police on Friday caught seven rebel Kurds they said were behind a suicide bomb attack on a crack police force headquarters that killed four people in the southern town of Adana.
A 17-year-old woman PKK guerrilla, dressed to look pregnant, blew up herself and four others in the attack last Friday -- the second of three such attacks by the rebel Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK).
Interior Minister Mehmet Agar said one of the detained men -- a 38-year-old codenamed "Isa", whom he identified as Bayram Yoruk -- had directly planned the attack and the other six had helped him.

"This man brought the terrorist girl to the scene of the incident at around 3 p.m. But the girl took fright and changed her mind about carrying out the attack," the Anatolian news agency quoted Agar as saying.
"He took the girl out of town and threatened her at gunpoint before taking her back some two hours later. And then the sad event took place," Agar said.

The men are currently detained in Adana. Police did not say when they expected the seven to be brought before a prosecutor for questioning. The prosecutor must then decide if he will charge them and what charges he will bring.
More than 21,000 people have died in the PKK's 12-year-old battle for self-rule in the mainly Kurdish southeast, but the suicide bombings only started this year.

The first attack came in July, after PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan warned of a wave of suicide bombings on the model of strikes by the Palestinian group Hamas. The latest was on Tuesday, the national holiday celebrating the founding of the Turkish republic in 1923.
All three attacks were staged by female militants dressed up as pregnant women with explosives strapped to their waist.
A police spokesman said security forces had found letters showing that the Adana bomber, Leyla Kaplan, had tried to leave the PKK and had been questioned and dissuaded by Yoruk.
"They caught them through letters and documents found at the woman bomber's house," a police spokesman in Adana told Reuters.
Agar said the PKK was using the suicide attacks as a way of punishing guerrillas it had decided to "eliminate" anyway.
He said Turkish security forces were working harder than ever to catch and punish all those directly and indirectly responsible for such actions.

"Whatever part of the world they may be, they will not escape being tracked," he said. "It is not possible to carry out such actions, discounting the lives of innocent people, and then just to retreat."
